If this document renders, your set-up works: Quarto ran Python, and polars, plotnine, great_tables and statsmodels all did their job on the Alpenglow data. The file stands alone: it needs no other file and reads the data from the course repository on GitHub (you need an internet connection).

**How to use it**

1. Open this file in Positron. If its folder has a `.venv`, pick **Python 3.14.8 (.venv)** at the top right: Quarto runs the file with that `.venv`, so the packages must go there.
2. Run the install cell below **once**: click into it and press Ctrl/Cmd + Enter. Quarto cannot install its own helpers while it renders, so this step comes first.
3. Press **Preview** (Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K).

Preview says *No module named 'yaml'* or *There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv*? Then the packages went to a different Python. Install them straight into the `.venv` from Positron's terminal, then preview again:

```bash
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install polars plotnine great-tables statsmodels pyarrow jupyter   # Windows
.venv/bin/python -m pip install polars plotnine great-tables statsmodels pyarrow jupyter         # macOS
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
# 1 Install (run once in Positron; Quarto skips this cell)
# The four course packages, plus pyarrow (polars uses it to hand data to
# plotnine and statsmodels) and jupyter (lets Quarto run Python).
%pip install polars plotnine great-tables statsmodels pyarrow jupyter
import sys
print("Installed into:", sys.executable)  # must end in .venv\Scripts\python.exe (macOS: .venv/bin/python)
```

```{python}
# 2 Load the packages
import polars as pl
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from great_tables import GT
from plotnine import aes, geom_line, ggplot, labs, theme_minimal
```

```{python}
# 3 polars: read the data and sum 2025 revenue by country
URL = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arnefloh-wu/"
       "international-marketing-analytics-teaching/main/data/mmm/alpenglow_weekly.csv")
sales = pl.read_csv(URL, try_parse_dates=True)
summary = (
    sales
    .filter(pl.col("week").dt.year() == 2025)
    .group_by("country")
    .agg(pl.col("revenue_eur_k").sum().alias("revenue_2025_eur_k"))
    .sort("revenue_2025_eur_k", descending=True)
)
```

```{python}
# 4 great_tables: the summary as a table
(GT(summary)
 .tab_header(title="Revenue by country, 2025", subtitle="thousand EUR")
 .fmt_number(columns="revenue_2025_eur_k", decimals=0))
```

```{python}
# 5 plotnine: weekly sales in Austria and Germany
two = sales.filter(pl.col("country").is_in(["AT", "DE"]))
(ggplot(two, aes("week", "sales_units_k", color="country"))
 + geom_line()
 + labs(x="", y="Weekly sales (thousand units)", color="")
 + theme_minimal())
```

```{python}
# 6 statsmodels: a regression for Austria
at = sales.filter(pl.col("country") == "AT").to_pandas()
model = smf.ols("sales_units_k ~ price_eur + spend_tv_k + spend_paid_search_k", data=at).fit()
model.params.round(2)
```

The model explains `{python} f"{model.rsquared:.0%}"` of the weekly variation in Austrian sales. If you can read this sentence with a number in it, your set-up works.
